Guadalajara, Mexico, April 30.— Pablo Yordi, the little Swiss, charged with swindling the Bank of Jalisco of this city, out of 61,006 pesos, and who was in the county jail at El Pasc tes many months pending the result 0! the™{ieht for extradition, is facing 4 term gf several years in the state penirentiey “~here. Under the state law, which proportions the’imprisonment tc the magnitude of the swindle, in case o! conviction, the maximum penalty in the Yordi case is nine years.

Yordi hag been identified by Bank of Jalisco officials and employes, by former employers and acquaintances, by lewyers, barbers, clerks and tailors, but his defence is that he was in El Paso, and not in Guadalejara at the time of the swindle, and that those testifring against him were mistaken. Yordi has employed an attorney and an effort to prove an alibi may be made, but such an attempt failed in El Paso.

Jury trials are unknown in this state, and judge Miramontes, of the first crimina! court. who has charge of tiv Yordi case, is judge, jury and proseruting attorney. He conducts all examinations, takes testimony and brine: tne prisoner and witnesses together. Judge Miramontes expects to conclud¢ the case early in May, and he. will th. turn over all testimony to the “prorurador de justicia,” cr public prosecutor, for review.

After reviewing the case, the proseeutor will ask that certain sentence be imposed. The criminal judge has the right to increase or lessen the penalty asked by the prosecutor. After sentence is passed in the criminal court, appeals can be taken, up to the supreme pourt of Mexico.
